articles.title: A North Carolina judge has blocked a farm owner’s plan to build a 2,500-seat amphitheater on Orange County farmland covered by a 187-acre conservation easement that a dairy family signed nearly 30 years ago
articles.summary: A long-running dispute over development on protected farmland in North Carolina has taken a significant turn after a Superior Court judge ruled in favour
articles.body: A long-running dispute over development on protected farmland in North Carolina has taken a significant turn after a Superior Court judge ruled in favour of a conservation group seeking to stop a proposed outdoor amphitheater. The October 15 decision effectively ends the prospect of a jury trial in the case, although the farm owner still has the option to appeal. According to reporting by The News & Observer, alongside earlier coverage by WRAL and Chapelboro, the dispute centres on Union Grove Farm in Orange County, where plans for a 2,500-seat entertainment venue have raised questions about land-use restrictions and the legal protection of agricultural landscapes. Superior Court Judge John Morris granted summary judgment in favour of Triangle Land Conservancy (TLC), the nonprofit that has been fighting the proposed development. The ruling was issued on October 15, ahead of a jury trial scheduled for November. Morris did not provide a detailed explanation of his decision in the reported proceedings. Union Grove Farm owner Greg Bohlen has 30 days to challenge the ruling before the North Carolina Court of Appeals.How the conservation dispute beganThe legal battle dates back to 1995, when Bob Nutter, the late owner of Maple View Dairy, entered into a 187-acre conservation easement with Triangle Land Conservancy. The agreement was designed to protect the property's agricultural productivity, open spaces and scenic character while restricting certain forms of construction and development.The Nutter family eventually sold the property, with Bohlen's companies and business partners acquiring the farm in 2021. The new owners subsequently established Union Grove Farm, focusing on regenerative agriculture and vineyard operations.Tensions escalated when the conservancy raised objections to three newly constructed roads crossing the protected land and the proposed amphitheater. In August 2025, TLC filed a lawsuit seeking to have the roads addressed and prevent the entertainment venue from being built. The organisation argued that the proposed development was inconsistent with the original conservation agreement, which was intended to protect the land in perpetuity.Why the amphitheater faced oppositionThe dispute also involved Orange County's rules governing agritourism, which allow qualifying farms to conduct certain public-facing activities without following standard county zoning requirements. However, in June 2025, the county's planning director determined that the proposed amphitheater did not qualify as an agritourism activity and could not proceed under that exemption. The decision also rejected plans for additional commercial facilities, including 10 cottages, a 40-room farm stay centre, event space and a restaurant.Bohlen initially challenged the planning director's decision but later withdrew his appeal before a scheduled Board of Adjustment hearing in October 2025. His legal team had indicated that the farm could explore a revised proposal with a smaller venue and different activities. That development did not resolve the separate conservation dispute. TLC continued pursuing its lawsuit, seeking a legal determination that the amphitheater violated the easement regardless of how the project was classified under county regulations.The farm's future and what happens nextUnion Grove Farm has also defended its wider agricultural operations, which include muscadine grape cultivation, sheep grazing and vermiculture, a process that uses worms to turn organic waste into compost. Bohlen, a fifth-generation farmer who previously worked in venture capital, has promoted regenerative farming as a way to improve soil health and create a more sustainable agricultural ecosystem. The farm's operations extend across more than 1,200 acres in the Dairyland Road community.The latest ruling also dismissed a counterclaim brought by East-West Organics, an entity associated with the neighbouring Center for Regenerative Agriculture, which had sought clarification about possible future development on its property. The decision follows another setback for Bohlen in June 2026, when a separate counterclaim against Triangle Land Conservancy was dismissed. That case involved disagreements over whether Union Grove Farm, as a tenant, had the authority to renegotiate the original conservation agreement on behalf of the property owners.For now, the October ruling represents a major victory for Triangle Land Conservancy, which oversees more than 200 conservation easements across the region. The organisation has indicated that it supports the farm's regenerative agricultural work and hopes to work towards restoring the protected property's conservation values. However, the possibility of an appeal means the legal dispute may not be entirely over. The timeline for restoring the affected land and resolving the remaining disagreements has yet to be established.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1978, barefoot forest ecologist Stephen King and fellow protesters camped in Pureora’s ancient tōtara canopy; logging was suspended in the occupied Pikiariki block
articles.summary: In January 1978, Stephen King and conservationists began a pioneering tree-sitting protest in Pureora Forest, halting logging efforts and preserving New Zealand's native forest ecosystems for future generations.
articles.body: Pureora is a forest in New Zealand’s central North Island, home to some of the country’s oldest tōtara and other podocarp trees, which rise above a dense understory. These forests are home to native birds that live beneath the canopy, including species that have disappeared from other areas. For most of the 20th century, the forests in the area were seen simply as timber waiting to be milled and this was common throughout the region. In the end, a small group of conservationists came to believe that protests and submissions were not stopping the logging quickly enough. Instead, they chose a tactic that was unusual in forest protection at the time: climbing into the tree canopy and staying there. Instead of placards, the protesters used climbing platforms and camping equipment, which made it difficult for loggers to cut down trees with people in them.Pureora before January 1978Dave Pye worked as a timber cruiser in Pureora Forest between 1962 and 1978. Conscious Explorer notes that without modern machinery, his work relied on an axe and a long saw. At the time, the only environmental group focused on forests was the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society, until the Beech Forest Action Committee emerged and later became the Native Forest Action Council, according to Te Ara, the government-run encyclopedia of New Zealand. The council pushed for legal recognition of native forest and campaigned to stop its logging.According to The New Zealand Herald, Stephen King was known as a barefoot forest ecologist and was involved with the council’s Auckland branch at the time of the protest. Conscious Explorer also notes that King gathered a petition against the logging of indigenous forest. Afterwards, King and his supporters submitted a lengthy report to Parliament on the declining numbers of rare birds such as the kōkako. King said that when the government did not meet their demands, they felt they had no other option but to climb the trees.The tree sit-in of 18 January 1978 and the logging halt that became permanent in 1982According to Te Ara, the Pureora tree-sitting protest began on 18 January 1978, when activists climbed into the trees and occupied them to prevent logging in the forest. According to Flight for the Forest, a book by Potton and Burton on environmental organisations, the Pureora protest was an early and significant tree-sitting action in New Zealand. The same source describes Prime Minister Robert Muldoon’s reluctance to stop the logging, despite pressure from the young protesters. The tree-sitters physically blocked logging in the occupied Pikiariki block and according to Te Ara, the government formally suspended it there later in 1978, with the halt becoming permanent in 1982.Pureora’s podocarp forests are among the oldest in the country. Trees such as tōtara, rimu and mataī can live for hundreds of years and they shelter species like the kōkako, a rare native bird known for its haunting song. For conservationists, that was exactly what was at stake: these were not just stands of timber but living habitats that, once felled, could not be replaced within a human lifetime. This is why the protesters were willing to give up the comfort of the ground and spend days on small platforms high above the forest floor. Their campaign drew national attention to a question that had been largely ignored until then: whether New Zealand’s remaining native forests should be milled at all.You use AI every day.
